questions.q: According to this lesson, why does building a golden record alone not finish the job?
options: Because the golden record provides no value until it actually reaches every system that consumes it
Because golden records automatically expire after creation
Because golden records can only be used by the system that built them
Because distribution is unrelated to master data management
questions.explain: Matching, deduplication, and survivorship produce a trusted record, but that work pays off only once e-commerce, billing, and other consuming systems actually receive the current version.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff between batch and real-time master data distribution, per this lesson?
options: Batch is simpler but leaves consumers stale between runs; real-time is more complex but avoids staleness where it would cause real harm
Batch distribution is always faster than real-time distribution
Real-time distribution requires no infrastructure at all
Batch distribution can only be used for customer master, never for other domains
questions.explain: Batch is acceptable for most reference and master data, but real-time is reserved for cases like a customer's credit hold status, where a delay could cause an order to ship that shouldn't.

questions.q: Why does point-to-point distribution become unmanageable as more consuming systems are added, according to this lesson?
options: Each new consumer requires building and maintaining its own custom integration with the system of record
Point-to-point distribution has a hard technical limit of exactly two systems
Point-to-point distribution is illegal under most data governance frameworks
Adding a consumer under point-to-point always deletes the previous integration
questions.explain: Under point-to-point, a tenth consuming system means building a tenth custom integration, and the source has to know every consumer's specific format — a burden that grows with each addition.

questions.q: How does publish-subscribe distribution address the scaling problem of point-to-point integration?
options: The source publishes updates to a central channel without needing to know who's listening, and new consumers simply subscribe
It requires the source system to build a new integration for every consumer, just like point-to-point
It eliminates the need for any consuming system to receive updates at all
It only works for exactly two systems, the same limit as point-to-point
questions.explain: Adding an eleventh consumer under publish-subscribe means that system subscribes to the channel — the publisher itself doesn't change, unlike point-to-point.

questions.q: What does this lesson say mature MDM programs monitor regarding distribution, beyond whether the source successfully sent an update?
options: Whether each consuming system actually received and applied the last update
Only the total number of updates sent per day, with no further detail
The individual salaries of the engineers who built the integration
Whether the update was sent in the correct programming language
questions.explain: A consumer can silently stop receiving updates due to a broken subscription or failed batch job, drifting out of sync invisibly — so monitoring confirms the update was actually applied, not just dispatched.
